title: 10. Real-time analytics (OLAP serving)
summary: A specialised serving store ingests events from Kafka within seconds and answers high-concurrency, sub-second aggregate queries, beside the lakehouse rather than instead of it.

blocks.text: 46.1 Context and the problem it solved

Warehouses and lakehouses are built for analysts: tens of concurrent users, queries taking seconds to minutes, data minutes to hours old. Some products need something else. A seller dashboard in a marketplace, an ad campaign console, a 'who viewed your profile' page or an operations control room serves thousands of users, each expecting results in under a second, on data a few seconds old.

Running that load on a general warehouse means huge warehouse sizes, per-query cost multiplied by page views, and latency that varies with cluster warm-up and caching. **Real-time OLAP stores** such as ClickHouse, Apache Pinot and Apache Druid emerged (several from LinkedIn, Uber, Yandex and ad-tech companies) to serve this pattern: continuous ingestion from streams, columnar storage with aggressive indexing and pre-aggregation, and query engines tuned for many small, fast, filtered aggregations.

blocks.title: Real-time serving beside the lakehouse
blocks.caption: The same Kafka topics also feed the Iceberg lakehouse (chapter 45).

blocks.title: Layers of a real-time analytics platform

layers.label: Query API
layers.sub: parameterised queries, tenant isolation, rate limits

layers.label: Real-time OLAP store
layers.sub: recent and hot data, rollups, indexes, upsert tables

layers.label: Lakehouse
layers.sub: Iceberg history, batch corrections, backfills, full-detail analytics

blocks.caption: The OLAP store serves; the lakehouse remains the system of record for analytics.

blocks.text: Events flow from Kafka directly into the OLAP store, which makes them queryable within seconds of arrival. Applications never query the store with free-form SQL from the browser: an API layer injects the tenant filter, limits time ranges, and caches popular results. The lakehouse keeps the complete history and feeds batch backfills or corrected data into the store when needed.

head: Layer
Component
Typical tools
rows: ClickHouse Kafka engine or ClickPipes, Pinot real-time tables, Druid Kafka indexing service
ClickHouse MergeTree family; Pinot segments with inverted, range and star-tree indexes; Druid segments with bitmap indexes
Rollups at ingestion or via views
ClickHouse materialized views into Summing/AggregatingMergeTree; Druid ingestion rollup; Pinot star-tree index
ClickHouse ReplacingMergeTree; Pinot upsert tables; Druid mostly re-ingests time intervals
Spark or ingestion jobs from Iceberg or Parquet; ClickHouse can also read Iceberg directly
Custom service, GraphQL layer, Cube with pre-aggregations

blocks.text: Snowflake offers options aimed at lower-latency workloads, such as hybrid tables for point reads and writes and newer interactive or low-latency query features. Their capabilities, limits and pricing change; check the current documentation and benchmark against your concurrency and latency targets before treating them as a replacement for a dedicated OLAP store.
46.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

Modelling is query-first and denormalised. Joins at query time are expensive or limited (Pinot and Druid have restricted join support; ClickHouse joins well when the right side is small), so dimensions are flattened into events at ingestion, often by a Flink job, and tables are sorted by the filters users always apply: tenant, then time.

items: **Rollups** pre-aggregate on ingestion: store counts and sums per minute per tenant per page instead of individual events. Rollups commonly reduce rows by 10-100x, at the cost of losing detail.
**Sort and primary keys** decide pruning. In ClickHouse, `ORDER BY (tenant_id, event_date, ...)` lets a tenant's query read a tiny fraction of the table.

**Upserts** are the hard part. ReplacingMergeTree deduplicates only at background merge time, so queries need `FINAL` or `argMax` patterns; Pinot upserts require the Kafka topic to be partitioned by the primary key.
**Medallion mapping:** the OLAP store is a gold-like serving layer fed from bronze or silver streams. It is not where conformance happens.

**Semantic layer:** a metric layer can target the OLAP store for user-facing metrics (Cube's pre-aggregations are a common pattern), but keep metric definitions shared with the lakehouse gold so numbers agree.

blocks.title: ClickHouse: Kafka ingestion with a per-minute rollup
blocks.text:
CREATE TABLE page_views_queue (
  tenant_id UInt32,
  page String,
  user_id String,
  ts DateTime
) ENGINE = Kafka
SETTINGS kafka_broker_list = 'kafka:9092',
         kafka_topic_list = 'web.page_views.v1',
         kafka_group_name = 'clickhouse_page_views',
         kafka_format = 'JSONEachRow';

CREATE TABLE page_views_1m (
  tenant_id UInt32,
  page String,
  minute DateTime,
  views UInt64
) ENGINE = SummingMergeTree
ORDER BY (tenant_id, minute, page);

CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW page_views_1m_mv TO page_views_1m AS
SELECT tenant_id, page, toStartOfMinute(ts) AS minute, count() AS views
FROM page_views_queue
GROUP BY tenant_id, page, minute;

-- merges are eventual: always re-aggregate when querying
SELECT page, sum(views) AS views
FROM page_views_1m
WHERE tenant_id = 42 AND minute >= now() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
GROUP BY page
ORDER BY views DESC
LIMIT 10;

Distinct counts cannot be summed across minutes. For unique users, store an aggregate state (for example `uniqState` in an AggregatingMergeTree, or a sketch such as HLL or Theta in Pinot and Druid) and merge it at query time.

Streaming ingestion is handled by the store itself, so there is little orchestration on the hot path. Orchestrated work lives around it: batch backfills from Iceberg when a stream bug is fixed, periodic compaction or segment merging, retention (for example 90 days hot in the store, all history in the lakehouse) and schema changes rolled out in step with Kafka schemas. Serving targets are typically p95 latencies of tens to a few hundred milliseconds at hundreds or thousands of queries per second.

Treating the OLAP store as a second warehouse. Teams add ad hoc joins, wide exploratory queries and long history until latency degrades for the customer-facing product. Keep exploration in the lakehouse and give the store a narrow, well-tested query surface.

head: Aspect
Strength
Weakness / failure mode
rows: Degrades sharply with unplanned joins or unfiltered scans
Ingestion lag spikes during rebalancing or backpressure
A second storage and operations stack to run
Eventual dedup, partitioning constraints, mutation cost
Numbers drift from gold if logic is duplicated
Poor for exploration and new questions

blocks.text: 46.7 When to choose it, and when not

items: Choose it for user-facing or operational analytics with many concurrent users and sub-second targets.
Choose it when freshness of seconds matters and data arrives through Kafka.
Choose it when query shapes are known and stable enough to design sort keys and rollups.
Avoid it for ad hoc analysis, complex multi-table modelling or full history; use the lakehouse or warehouse.
Avoid it when a few dozen internal users can wait seconds; a well-sized warehouse with caching is simpler.
Coexist: Kafka feeds both; the lakehouse owns history and definitions; the store owns the hot window.

blocks.title: Seller analytics in a marketplace
blocks.text: A marketplace offered 200,000 sellers a dashboard of views, orders and conversion. Running it on the warehouse cost more each month than the feature earned and showed 30-second spinners. The team fed Kafka page-view and order events into ClickHouse with per-minute rollups ordered by seller and time, kept 13 months hot, and served queries through an API that enforces the seller filter.
items: p95 latency fell below 200 ms at peak
Conversion definition was shared with the lakehouse gold model and reconciled daily
A pricing bug was corrected by re-ingesting two days from Iceberg

blocks.title: Add real-time serving to a lakehouse
blocks.text: A ride-hailing company has an Iceberg lakehouse fed by Kafka. City operations want a live map dashboard of trips, supply and surge per zone, refreshed every 5 seconds for 2,000 users, and drivers want an earnings screen showing today's trips. Choose an OLAP store, define table grain, sort keys and rollups, decide how corrections (refunds, cancelled trips) are applied, and explain how numbers stay consistent with finance reports from the lakehouse.
hints: Earnings need per-trip state that changes; zone metrics do not
Which store handles upserts by key, and with what constraints?
Where should the definition of 'completed trip' live?

items: Real-time OLAP stores serve high-concurrency, sub-second queries on seconds-fresh data.
ClickHouse, Pinot and Druid ingest from Kafka natively and rely on sort keys, indexes and rollups.
Model query-first: denormalise, sort by tenant and time, pre-aggregate, use sketches for distinct counts.
Upserts exist but carry constraints; check each store's semantics.
The store complements the lakehouse: Kafka feeds both, the lakehouse keeps history and shared definitions.

blocks.q: Why does the ClickHouse query on a SummingMergeTree table still use sum(views) with GROUP BY?
options: Because background merges are eventual, so several partial rows per key may exist at query time
Because the Kafka engine duplicates every row
Because SummingMergeTree stores only raw events
Because ClickHouse cannot read materialized views directly
blocks.explain: Rows are combined only when parts merge, which happens asynchronously. Queries must re-aggregate to be correct; the table already holds rolled-up rows, not raw events.

blocks.q: How should unique visitors per hour be computed from per-minute rollups?
options: Store a mergeable sketch or aggregate state per minute and merge it at query time
Recompute from the warehouse on every request
blocks.explain: The same user can appear in many minutes, so summing distinct counts overcounts. Mergeable states (uniqState, HLL, Theta) combine correctly; going back to the warehouse defeats the serving store.

blocks.q: What is a requirement for Apache Pinot upsert tables?
options: Data must be loaded only in batch
The input stream must be partitioned by the primary key
blocks.explain: Pinot tracks the latest record per key within a partition, so all records for a key must arrive in the same stream partition. Upserts apply to real-time tables, not batch-only ones.

blocks.q: An internal team of 30 analysts wants faster dashboards on data refreshed hourly. What is the most reasonable first step?
options: Tune the warehouse or lakehouse gold tables and caching before adding a new store
Deploy Apache Druid fed from Kafka
blocks.explain: Low concurrency and hourly freshness do not need a dedicated OLAP stack. Adding one brings a second system to operate and a risk of drifting definitions.
